---
title: "Dog names, generations and neighborhood income"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
    toc: true
    df-print: paged
execute:
  echo: true
  message: false
---

Do dogs in higher- and lower-income NYC neighborhoods have different names? Do their names also differ in which baby-name decades they match?

The motivating idea is that names might move between social groups and eventually become dog names. The comparisons here can describe generational and neighborhood patterns. Demonstrating that diffusion would require evidence of human naming by income and dog-name adoption over time.

## Packages and helpers
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
source("R/helpers.R")
```

## Read the prepared tables
```{r}
#| label: read-prepared-tables
dogs_prepared <- read_csv(
  "data/derived/dogs_prepared_2024.csv", na = "",
  col_types = cols(
    zipcode = col_character(),
    birth_year = col_character(), .default = col_guess()
  )
)
ssa_reference <- read_csv("data/derived/ssa_name_reference.csv", na = "", show_col_types = FALSE)
zip_income <- read_csv(
  "data/lookups/zip_zcta_income_ny_acs2024.csv", na = "",
  col_types = cols(zip_code = col_character(), zcta = col_character(), .default = col_guess())
)
nyc_areas <- read_csv("data/raw/nyc-zcta-list.csv", col_types = cols(zcta5 = col_character()))
```

## Match baby names to dogs
Use all complete decades in the reference. Keep a separate yes/no result for each decade so a name can match several generations.
```{r}
#| label: match-dogs-to-baby-names
ssa_reference |>
  select(name, ssa_recognized, starts_with("top100_")) ->
  ssa_name_flags

ssa_name_flags |>
  select(-name) |>
  names() ->
  name_flags

dogs_prepared |>
  left_join(ssa_name_flags, by = "name") |>
  mutate(across(all_of(name_flags), function(name_matches) replace_na(name_matches, FALSE))) ->
  dogs

dogs |>
  select(name, ssa_recognized, starts_with("top100_")) |>
  preview()
```

## Attach neighborhood income
Match the recorded owner's ZIP to Shweta's ZIP-to-ZCTA income table. Several ZIPs can share one Census area, or ZCTA. The income describes that whole area, not the owner's personal wealth.

Keep an exact numeric estimate only when one is supplied. For `top_coded` areas, the income is $250,000 or more; the exact amount is unknown. These dogs remain eligible, and the status will place them in the highest income group. The saved lookup's `250001` is a reporting code, not an exact income.
```{r}
#| label: attach-neighborhood-income
zip_income |>
  select(
    zipcode = zip_code, lookup_state = state, post_office = po_name, zcta,
    median_household_income = median_hh_income,
    income_margin_of_error = median_hh_income_moe,
    income_status, acs_release, acs_period
  ) |>
  mutate(median_household_income = if_else(income_status == "estimate", median_household_income, NA_real_)) ->
  income_reference

dogs |>
  left_join(income_reference, by = "zipcode") ->
  dogs_with_income
```

## Select the NYC comparison
Use the city's published ZCTA list as our study boundary. Some listed areas extend outside NYC; we accept that overlap because a ZIP alone cannot locate each owner within the area. The results describe dogs with recorded ZIPs mapping to this selected set of areas, rather than a precise census of dogs living inside the municipal boundary.

Check whether each ZIP matched the lookup, whether its area is on the city list, and whether income information is available. `is.element()` checks membership in a list. The income statuses include the open-ended highest and lowest amounts; an exact numeric estimate is not required for inclusion.
```{r}
#| label: identify-income-comparison-records
nyc_areas |>
  pull(zcta5) ->
  nyc_area_codes

dogs_with_income |>
  pull(lookup_state) |>
  is.na() ->
  zipcode_unmatched

dogs_with_income |>
  pull(zcta) |>
  is.element(nyc_area_codes) ->
  area_on_city_list

dogs_with_income |>
  pull(income_status) |>
  is.element(c("estimate", "top_coded", "bottom_coded")) ->
  income_available

dogs_with_income |>
  mutate(
    income_comparison_status = case_when(
      zipcode_unmatched ~ "zip_not_in_ny_lookup",
      !area_on_city_list ~ "outside_nyc_area_list",
      !income_available ~ "income_unavailable",
      TRUE ~ "included"
    )
  ) ->
  dogs_with_comparison_status
```

Report the exclusions, then keep the same selected dogs for all comparisons below. The status column serves this report and is left out of the selected dog table.
```{r}
#| label: keep-income-comparison-records
dogs_with_comparison_status |>
  count(income_comparison_status, name = "estimated_dogs") ->
  income_comparison_counts

dogs_with_comparison_status |>
  filter(income_comparison_status != "included") |>
  select(
    estimated_dog_id, source_row_id, name, zipcode, zcta, post_office,
    income_status, exclusion_reason = income_comparison_status
  ) ->
  income_exclusions

dogs_with_comparison_status |>
  filter(income_comparison_status == "included") |>
  select(-income_comparison_status, -lookup_state, -post_office) ->
  dogs_in_selected_areas

income_comparison_counts
```

This retains 92,547 estimated dogs, including 364 with incomes reported as $250,000+. The other 380 are recorded in the exclusion table. An outside-city ZIP does not tell us whether the owner moved, has another residence, or supplied a different address. These exclusions limit which dogs our findings describe.

## Group neighborhoods by income
Use four bands of area median household income: under $50,000, $50,000–99,999, $100,000–149,999 and $150,000+. An estimate exactly on a boundary enters the higher band. Handle open-ended amounts first so the $250,000+ cases remain in the highest group despite having no exact numeric estimate. These bands describe areas, not individual owners' incomes or social classes.

The labels below define their display order. `factor()` keeps that order when grouping or plotting, rather than sorting the labels alphabetically.
```{r}
#| label: assign-income-groups
income_group_labels <- c(
  "Under $50,000", "$50,000–99,999", "$100,000–149,999", "$150,000+"
)

dogs_in_selected_areas |>
  mutate(
    income_group = case_when(
      income_status == "top_coded" ~ "$150,000+",
      income_status == "bottom_coded" ~ "Under $50,000",
      median_household_income < 50000 ~ "Under $50,000",
      median_household_income < 100000 ~ "$50,000–99,999",
      median_household_income < 150000 ~ "$100,000–149,999",
      TRUE ~ "$150,000+"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(income_group = factor(income_group, levels = income_group_labels)) ->
  dogs_for_income_comparison

dogs_for_income_comparison |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarise(dogs = n(), neighborhoods = n_distinct(zcta), .groups = "drop") ->
  income_group_counts

income_group_counts
```

## Compare counting units
Compare the proportion of matching names when each dog counts once with the proportion when each license counts once. Both calculations use the same selected NYC-area dogs with income information. This checks the effect of repeat licenses; the income-group comparison below counts every dog once. `across()` repeats the same calculation for every name flag.
```{r}
#| label: compare-counting-units
dogs_for_income_comparison |>
  summarise(across(all_of(name_flags), mean)) |>
  mutate(unit = "estimated_dog") ->
  dog_matching_rates

dogs_for_income_comparison |>
  summarise(across(all_of(name_flags), function(name_matches) {
    weighted.mean(name_matches, license_record_count)
  })) |>
  mutate(unit = "named_license_record") ->
  license_matching_rates

dog_matching_rates |>
  bind_rows(license_matching_rates) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(name_flags), names_to = "measure", values_to = "share") |>
  select(unit, measure, share) ->
  matching_comparison

matching_comparison
```

## Compare naming patterns across income groups
Count every estimated dog once within its income group. For each baby-name decade, count dogs whose names match that decade's top 100 and divide by all selected dogs in the income group. Neighborhoods with more recorded dogs contribute more to the result. A name can match several decades, so the decade percentages need not add to 100%.

The separate `ssa_recognized` measure asks whether a name appears anywhere in the baby-name reference. It does not identify names given by wealthy parents: the SSA reference contains national name counts by year, not parents' incomes.
```{r}
#| label: compare-name-matches-by-income
dogs_for_income_comparison |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(name_flags), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(name_flags), names_to = "name_measure", values_to = "matching_dogs") |>
  left_join(income_group_counts, by = "income_group") |>
  mutate(share = matching_dogs / dogs) ->
  name_matches_by_income
```

Neighborhood income describes the area associated with the recorded owner's ZIP. These shares describe whether dog names and their baby-name generations differ across area-income groups. They cannot establish a chain of names moving from wealthy families to poorer families and then to dogs.

## Compare baby-name decades
The horizontal axis describes when the baby names were popular. Every point uses the same 2024 dog snapshot; the lines do not show dog names changing over time. Each income group keeps the same color in both charts.
```{r}
#| label: plot-baby-name-decades
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
income_group_colors <- c("#D55E00", "#009E73", "#0072B2", "#7B4B94")

name_matches_by_income |>
  filter(name_measure != "ssa_recognized") |>
  mutate(decade = str_remove(name_measure, "top100_")) |>
  mutate(decade = as.integer(decade)) ->
  decade_matches

decade_matches |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = share, color = income_group, linetype = income_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = income_group_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1880, 2010, by = 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 0.08)) +
  labs(
    title = "Dog names and baby-name decades",
    subtitle = "Share of dogs matching each decade's U.S. top 100 baby names",
    x = "Baby-name decade (starting year)", y = "Share of dogs in the income group",
    color = "Area median household income", linetype = "Area median household income",
    caption = "2024 NYC-area licenses | 92,547 estimated dogs | Each dog counts equally.\nA dog can match several decades; these percentages do not add to 100%."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)
  ) ->
  decade_comparison_plot

decade_comparison_plot
```

The higher-income groups have larger matching shares for every decade from the 1880s through the 1950s. For the 1880s list, the lowest and highest groups match 3.5% and 7.0%; for the 1920s, they match 1.8% and 4.2%. All four groups dip around the 1960s–1980s and rise for the 2000s–2010s. The recent decades do not follow a consistent income order. SSA's early birth records are less complete, so these are comparisons with the published lists, not perfect measures of historical naming.

## Compare overall baby-name recognition
This broader measure includes any name published in the SSA reference for 1880–2019, even if it never reached a decade's top 100. An unmatched name is not necessarily unused by people; it is absent from our reference under the chosen matching rules.
```{r}
#| label: plot-overall-baby-name-recognition
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
name_matches_by_income |>
  filter(name_measure == "ssa_recognized") |>
  mutate(percentage_label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)) ->
  overall_recognition

overall_recognition |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income_group, y = share, fill = income_group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percentage_label), vjust = -0.6, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = income_group_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Most dogs have a name found in the baby-name reference",
    subtitle = "Share matching any published U.S. baby name from 1880–2019",
    x = "Area median household income", y = "Share of dogs in the income group",
    caption = "2024 NYC-area licenses | 92,547 estimated dogs | Each dog counts equally.\nThis includes uncommon baby names, not only the top 100."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)
  ) ->
  overall_recognition_plot

overall_recognition_plot
```

Recognition rises across the four income groups: 78.1%, 79.8%, 80.6% and 82.1%. The highest-minus-lowest difference, calculated from the unrounded shares, is 4.1 percentage points. Most dogs in every group match the broad reference. The individual-name comparisons below show which names contribute to the differences; the charts alone do not show why owners chose them.

## Look at the actual dog names
Count names within each income group and divide by all dogs in that group. Rank by the count, breaking ties alphabetically. This lets us compare common names without letting the larger groups dominate through their raw counts.
```{r}
#| label: count-dog-names-by-income
dogs_for_income_comparison |>
  count(income_group, name, name = "dogs_with_name") |>
  left_join(income_group_counts, by = "income_group") |>
  mutate(share = dogs_with_name / dogs) |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  arrange(desc(dogs_with_name), name, .by_group = TRUE, .locale = "C") |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() ->
  dog_names_by_income

dog_names_by_income |>
  filter(rank <= 10) |>
  select(income_group, rank, name, dogs_with_name, share)
```

LUNA is the most common name in every income group. CHARLIE ranks ninth in the lowest group and second in the highest. Many names are shared across groups; the comparison concerns differences in frequency, not separate sets of names.

## Find names contributing to the decade differences
Compare the highest and lowest income groups name by name. A positive difference means the name is more common in the highest group. Multiply the difference in shares by 100 to express it in percentage points. If a name occurs in only one group, `values_fill = 0` supplies zero for the other group.
```{r}
#| label: compare-individual-name-shares
dog_names_by_income |>
  filter(income_group == "Under $50,000" | income_group == "$150,000+") |>
  mutate(comparison_group = if_else(
    income_group == "Under $50,000", "lowest_income_share", "highest_income_share"
  )) |>
  select(name, comparison_group, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = comparison_group, values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(difference_percentage_points = 100 * (highest_income_share - lowest_income_share)) ->
  name_share_differences

ssa_name_flags |>
  select(name, starts_with("top100_")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("top100_"), names_to = "name_measure", values_to = "in_top100") |>
  filter(in_top100) |>
  select(-in_top100) ->
  top_names_by_decade

name_share_differences |>
  inner_join(top_names_by_decade, by = "name") |>
  arrange(name_measure, desc(difference_percentage_points), name, .locale = "C") ->
  decade_name_contributions
```

Each name appears once for each decade it matches. Adding all its decade's positive and negative contributions gives that decade's highest-minus-lowest group difference. Keep contributions for all 14 decades; display the five largest positive contributions for the 1880s and 1920s as examples from the chart.
```{r}
#| label: inspect-older-name-contributions
decade_name_contributions |>
  filter(name_measure == "top100_1880" | name_measure == "top100_1920") |>
  group_by(name_measure) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  ungroup()
```

DAISY, HENRY, STELLA, GEORGE and LUCY together account for about 41% of the 1880s gap. HENRY, GEORGE, RUBY, HARRY and BETTY account for about 42% of the 1920s gap. Neither gap comes from a single name. The same name can contribute to several decades: HENRY is also in the 2010s top 100. A match to an old list does not establish that the name is exclusively old-fashioned or that an owner took it from that era.

## Look across neighborhoods
Calculate the same shares separately within each Census area. This shows whether the pooled income-group results describe every neighborhood or conceal variation. The main charts still count every dog equally; this table does not replace them with equal-neighborhood weighting.
```{r}
#| label: compare-name-matches-by-neighborhood
dogs_for_income_comparison |>
  group_by(income_group, zcta) |>
  summarise(dogs = n(), across(all_of(name_flags), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(name_flags), names_to = "name_measure", values_to = "matching_dogs") |>
  mutate(share = matching_dogs / dogs) ->
  name_matches_by_neighborhood

name_matches_by_neighborhood |>
  filter(name_measure == "top100_1880" | name_measure == "top100_1920") |>
  group_by(name_measure, income_group) |>
  summarise(
    neighborhoods = n(),
    median_neighborhood_share = median(share),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The median describes the middle neighborhood's share, rather than the pooled share of dogs. It rises across the four income bands for both displayed decades. For the 1880s it is 3.0%, 4.3%, 5.3% and 6.7%; for the 1920s it is 1.6%, 2.1%, 2.5% and 4.1%. Neighborhoods still overlap: area income does not determine an individual dog's name. Small areas can also have unstable percentages when only a few dogs contribute.

## What this first pass establishes
In this selected 2024 licensed-dog sample, neighborhood income is associated with naming differences. The oldest top-100 comparison is about twice as common in the highest income group, but the absolute gap is about 3.6 dogs per 100: 7.03% compared with 3.45%. Most dogs in both groups do not match that list.

Overall recognition is broader than a judgment that a name sounds human. For example, ROCKY, LUCKY and BUDDY all occur in the SSA reference. The four-percentage-point recognition gap therefore measures overlap with published baby names, not owners' intentions.

The charts cannot choose between diffusion, continuing use of classic names, revivals, or other differences between neighborhoods. We have no parents' income data, no record of how owners chose names, and no history of when each name became a dog name. The observed associations are descriptive; they do not establish a causal effect, statistical significance, or a pattern covering unlicensed dogs. The next review concerns whether the code and explanations make these measured comparisons clear and whether the collaborators agree on their use.

## Save the charts
Save a PNG copy of each chart in `figures` for review without rendering HTML. `dir.create()` makes that output folder if it does not already exist.
```{r}
#| label: save-name-comparison-charts
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave("figures/baby-name-decades-by-income.png", plot = decade_comparison_plot, width = 12, height = 7, dpi = 180, bg = "white")
ggsave("figures/baby-name-recognition-by-income.png", plot = overall_recognition_plot, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 180, bg = "white")
```

```{r}
#| label: save-matched-dogs
write_csv(dogs, "data/derived/dogs_2024.csv", na = "")
write_csv(dogs_for_income_comparison, "data/derived/dogs_income_2024.csv", na = "")
write_csv(income_exclusions, "data/derived/income_exclusions.csv", na = "")
write_csv(income_comparison_counts, "data/derived/income_comparison_counts.csv", na = "")
write_csv(income_group_counts, "data/derived/income_group_counts.csv", na = "")
write_csv(matching_comparison, "data/derived/matching_by_counting_unit.csv", na = "")
write_csv(name_matches_by_income, "data/derived/name_matches_by_income.csv", na = "")
write_csv(dog_names_by_income, "data/derived/dog_names_by_income.csv", na = "")
write_csv(decade_name_contributions, "data/derived/decade_name_contributions.csv", na = "")
write_csv(name_matches_by_neighborhood, "data/derived/name_matches_by_neighborhood.csv", na = "")
```
